content.content:
# JusPrin 2 pricing: the mental model (working doc, 2026-10-29)

Untracked working document for the pricing brainstorm. Facts, hypotheses, goal and comparables, kept apart on purpose. No recommendations here. Companion data: `v1-pricing-data-2026-10.md` (JusPrin v1 production data) and `obico-pro-pricing-data-2026-10.md` (Obico Pro production data, same audience).

Sourcing rule for the comparables: every figure comes from a page fetched or a search result read on 2026-10-29 by a research agent. "Vendor" marks a company's own page; "3P, loosely held" marks a third-party tracker, blog or news summary. Items from the original case list that no source supported are struck and listed at the end.

## Goal (Kenneth's words)

Traction, measured as active users and time in the app. Become the default AI harness for 3D slicing. Reduce friction as long as no choice now blocks turning profitable later. Collect feedback good enough to fine-tune small models later; willing to subsidise model cost to get it. The two audiences (people who already slice in OrcaSlicer, people who cannot) are believed to overlap heavily and converge. Sign-in is not required when the person uses their own API key.

Not yet decided: the traction number and horizon.

## Hypotheses

Each is a hypothesis until the named check is done. Survey evidence is noted where it bears on one.

1. **A premium chat costs $0.20 to $0.50 for a simple case.** Kenneth's estimate. Measured 2026-10-28 on Opus 5.5 in three harness chats: $0.30, $0.43 and $0.56. **Measured 2026-10-30 on Opus 5.5, pictures on, source at `2f9d322dee` (`journey-cost-2026-10.md`), one run each:** a simple 3-turn session $0.30, which fits, but a 5-turn troubleshooting session $0.64 ($0.66 with a photo) and a 6-turn complex session $1.27 do not. These are sessions with several turns and slices, so the range holds for the simple case only. Scripted turns follow within seconds; a person who pauses over 5 minutes before every turn would pay about $0.64, $2.56 and $1.49 (calculated from the logs, not measured), because Anthropic's cache lasts 5 minutes and rewriting it is the largest cost. **Measured 2026-11-01 on Claude Sonnet 5.5, pictures on, same scripted words, source `69780c7af4` plus the harness fix `01ec46a4af` (a newer build than the Opus runs; `journey-cost-2026-10.md`, "Sonnet 5.5, added 2026-11-01"), one run each:** the same sessions cost $0.19 (simple, 3 turns), $0.34 (complex, 6 turns) and $0.35 ($0.37 with the photo, troubleshooting, 5 turns), priced at Sonnet 5.5's rates of $2 input, $0.10 cache read, $2.50 five-minute cache write and $10 output per million tokens (fetched 2026-11-01). That is 0.64, 0.26 and 0.55 (0.56 with photo) of Opus's cost, and 0.40 over all 14 user messages ($0.063 a message against Opus's $0.158 and DeepSeek's $0.024). So the assumption that a Sonnet-class expert tier costs about half of Opus holds on two sessions (0.55 to 0.64, because Sonnet used 11 to 28% more tokens than Opus on the same words) and is pessimistic on the third (0.26, because Opus's complex run paid a $0.36 cache expiry during a slow slice and Sonnet's did not). The simple Sonnet session ($0.19) is just under the $0.20 to $0.50 range; the troubleshooting and complex sessions ($0.35, $0.34) fall inside it. Caveat: the Opus and Sonnet runs used different builds, and I did not run Opus on the new one. Check: gateway token accounting on real v2 chats, including real pauses.
2. **A cheap model costs roughly 15 to 30 times less per chat.** Guess from memory. **Measured 2026-10-30, same build, DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter with pictures removed, one run each:** $0.015, $0.31 and $0.020 against Opus's $0.30, $1.27 and $0.64, so 20 times, 4 times and 33 times less. The 4 times is the complex session, where DeepSeek polled the slicer 75 times during a slow slice on a debug build; those requests were two thirds of its cost, and without them the ratio is about 12 times (calculated). Answer quality was not compared. Check: gateway accounting on a shipped build, and whether the polling can be stopped.
3. **An engaged v2 user's monthly usage is unknown, and v1's overall medians do not estimate it.** Earlier versions of this model used v1's median payer (6.5 chats per 30 days) as "typical demand" and concluded a sub-$10 all-premium plan was profitable for most payers. That was wrong: the medians describe people who had stopped using v1. Using the first paid month instead (median 17.5 chats, 90th percentile 51 per 30 days) and Kenneth's $0.35 per chat, an engaged month costs about $6 at the median and $18 at the 90th percentile, so a $7 flat all-premium plan sits at break-even for the engaged median and underwater for the engaged tail. Kenneth's expectation (confirmed 2026-10-29): an engaged v2 user will use more than v1's first paid month showed, because v1's low numbers came from people leaving. So v1's first month is a floor for engaged usage, not an estimate, and v2 starts chats on file open and runs tools, which pushes the same way. Consequence: at $0.35 a chat an engaged user costs more than $6 a month on a frontier model, so a sub-$10 all-premium flat plan is underwater for engaged people from the start, and the cheap model or a budget is a launch question, not a later one. With the 2026-10-30 session measurements (Opus 5.5 $0.30 for a simple session, $0.64 for troubleshooting, $1.27 for a complex one, before real pauses), the same floor month costs $5 to $22 at the median of 17.5 sessions and $15 to $65 at the 90th percentile of 51, depending on the mix; on DeepSeek V4 Flash the same months cost $0.26 to $5.40 and $0.77 to $16, with the complex-session figure inflated by slice polling on a debug build. Check: beta cohort on the live gateway, measured on people still active in month two.
4. **The cheap model is good enough for the basic job.** Untested on the real task. Check: prompt eval harness vs Sonnet on print-setup cases, with image handling, at approved spend.
5. **A visible cap becomes a break-even anchor.** Supported in part: Midjourney users plan their month around hours. Refined by the survey: the anger spike in every case is at the boundary (silent swaps, meters disagreeing with cutoffs, "slower" turning into a wall), not at the number itself.
6. **A fallback keeps the session and still converts; a wall ends it.** ChatGPT and Gemini both degrade rather than stop, and the complaints are about the swap being silent. Unmeasured whether a fallback converts.
7. **Behaviour carries training signal for free, and rewarded explicit feedback from this audience is high quality.** The first half is supported by v1 (about 3,000 corrective follow-ups against 16 ratings) and by the surveyed cases that published measured gains (Duolingo, Cursor Tab). The second half comes from Obico's own rewarded print-shot labelling, which Kenneth reports produced good data. An earlier version of this hypothesis said rewards invite gaming; the survey did not support that. It found no evidence either way on Midjourney's rating data, one gamed gate at Tesla that was an access score rather than a reward for feedback, and a general warning from the Open Data Institute about leaderboards. That was one case and a caution, overstated into a pattern. Possible reasons Obico's result differs from the general worry, all untested: makers are a more conscientious population, and a small company's reward feels like a fair trade rather than something to exploit. The open question is no longer whether to reward feedback but what to ask, when, and how the reward relates to the missing label, "did the print work".
8. **The two audiences overlap and converge.** Kenneth's guess. Check: segment v1 users by whether they edit settings themselves.
9. **The July 2025 usage drop was launch decay, not the paywall.** My reading. Check: the July cohort's later behaviour.
10. **Grandfathering early payers is cheap.** True at tens of payers by arithmetic.
11. **The user base is heavily Brazilian; failed renewals are payment-method failures.** Half confirmed: v1 users are 35% US and 10% Brazil, but v1 payers are 16 of 34 Brazilian and 10 of 15 failed renewals were Brazilian cards. The payment-method mechanism is still unconfirmed: Chargebee records only "card declined" and "insufficient funds", never whether a cross-border or recurring charge was refused. Obico, 64% US payers, loses 30% of cancellations to failed payments too, so part of v1's rate is ordinary.
19. **New from Obico: a trial end converts more reliably than a usage cap.** Obico's lifetime conversion is 5%, and nearly half of its payers paid within the automatic trial window; v1 converted 0.7%, at a cap that 1% of months reach. Untested whether a trial works here: v1's median first week was 2.5 chats, but that median includes the 41% who never came back, so an engaged person's first week is unknown and almost certainly busier.
20. **New from Obico: the leading stated reason for cancelling is not using the product, far ahead of price.** This fits v1's silent later months. It is a hypothesis that a plan costing nothing in idle months (prepaid, usage-based, or annual priced for insurance) retains better than monthly; Obico's 77% annual renewal despite half-silent month 12 is the one data point.
21. **New from Obico: conversion in this audience fell four-fold after 2022 for unknown reasons**, while signups grew. Whatever caused it may bear on JusPrin's funnel too; nothing here tests the printer-camera explanation.
12. **New from the survey: "unlimited" survives only where marginal cost is near zero** (idle GPU queue, tab completions, own small models). No surveyed vendor offers unlimited frontier chat. For JusPrin this holds until the own-model phase.
13. **New: flat-fee hosted inference on rented frontier models gets repriced within about a year** (Zed) or the business leaves (Roo, Continue). Observed in daily-use professional tools with high token volume; a hobbyist slicer's volume is far lower, so the dynamic may not apply at the same scale.
14. **New: free tiers in costly-generation tools gate the artefact, not the generation** (download, export, commercial rights). A slicer chat has no equivalent artefact; the question is whether anything in JusPrin plays that role.
15. **New: a daily reset fits bursty hobby use better than a monthly one** (Suno). Untested here; v1 bursts are multi-day project sessions, not single days.
16. **New: "beta" or "trial" wording on a free allowance keeps the option to change it** (CapCut, Adobe's unenforced credits). Adobe shows the cost: the later enforcement was read as a bait and switch.
17. **New: seasonal hobby apps make annual the default and keep the person's own data free on lapse** (Strava, onX). v1's annual payers used about 33 chats a year against $59.99, a churn-shaped average (most of those years went quiet after the first month), not what an engaged year looks like.

Untracked working document for the pricing brainstorm. Facts, hypotheses, goal and comparables, kept apart on purpose. No recommendations here. Companion data: `v1-pricing-data-2026-10.md` (JusPrin v1 production data) and `obico-pro-pricing-data-2026-10.md` (Obico Pro production data, same audience).

Sourcing rule for the comparables: every figure comes from a page fetched or a search result read on 2026-10-29 by a research agent. "Vendor" marks a company's own page; "3P, loosely held" marks a third-party tracker, blog or news summary. Items from the original case list that no source supported are struck and listed at the end.

## Goal (Kenneth's words)

Traction, measured as active users and time in the app. Become the default AI harness for 3D slicing. Reduce friction as long as no choice now blocks turning profitable later. The two audiences (people who already slice in OrcaSlicer, people who cannot) are believed to overlap heavily and converge. Sign-in is not required when the person uses their own API key.

Not yet decided: the traction number and horizon.

Each is a hypothesis until the named check is done. Survey evidence is noted where it bears on one.

1. **A premium chat costs $0.20 to $0.50 for a simple case.** Kenneth's estimate. These are sessions with several turns and slices, so the range holds for the simple case only. Scripted turns follow within seconds; a person who pauses over 5 minutes before every turn would pay about $0.64, $2.56 and $1.49 (calculated from the logs, not measured), because Anthropic's cache lasts 5 minutes and rewriting it is the largest cost. **Measured 2026-11-01 on Claude Sonnet 5.5, pictures on, same scripted words, source `69780c7af4` plus the harness fix `01ec46a4af` (a newer build than the Opus runs; `journey-cost-2026-10.md`, "Sonnet 5.5, added 2026-11-01"), one run each:** the same sessions cost $0.19 (simple, 3 turns), $0.34 (complex, 6 turns) and $0.35 ($0.37 with the photo, troubleshooting, 5 turns), priced at Sonnet 5.5's rates of $2 input, $0.10 cache read, $2.50 five-minute cache write and $10 output per million tokens (fetched 2026-11-01). That is 0.64, 0.26 and 0.55 (0.56 with photo) of Opus's cost, and 0.40 over all 14 user messages ($0.063 a message against Opus's $0.158 and DeepSeek's $0.024). So the assumption that a Sonnet-class expert tier costs about half of Opus holds on two sessions (0.55 to 0.64, because Sonnet used 11 to 28% more tokens than Opus on the same words) and is pessimistic on the third (0.26, because Opus's complex run paid a $0.36 cache expiry during a slow slice and Sonnet's did not). The simple Sonnet session ($0.19) is just under the $0.20 to $0.50 range; the troubleshooting and complex sessions ($0.35, $0.34) fall inside it. Caveat: the Opus and Sonnet runs used different builds, and I did not run Opus on the new one. Check: gateway token accounting on real v2 chats, including real pauses.
2. **A cheap model costs roughly 15 to 30 times less per chat.** Guess from memory. **Measured 2026-10-30, same build, DeepSeek V4 Flash through OpenRouter with pictures removed, one run each:** $0.015, $0.31 and $0.020 against Opus's $0.30, $1.27 and $0.64, so 20 times, 4 times and 33 times less. The 4 times is the complex session, where DeepSeek polled the slicer 75 times during a slow slice on a debug build; those requests were two thirds of its cost, and without them the ratio is about 12 times (calculated). Answer quality was not compared. Check: gateway accounting on a shipped build, and whether the polling can be stopped.
3. **An engaged v2 user's monthly usage is unknown, and v1's overall medians do not estimate it.** Earlier versions of this model used v1's median payer (6.5 chats per 30 days) as "typical demand" and concluded a sub-$10 all-premium plan was profitable for most payers. That was wrong: the medians describe people who had stopped using v1. Using the first paid month instead (median 17.5 chats, 90th percentile 51 per 30 days) and Kenneth's $0.35 per chat, an engaged month costs about $6 at the median and $18 at the 90th percentile, so a $7 flat all-premium plan sits at break-even for the engaged median and underwater for the engaged tail. Kenneth's expectation (confirmed 2026-10-29): an engaged v2 user will use more than v1's first paid month showed, because v1's low numbers came from people leaving. So v1's first month is a floor for engaged usage, not an estimate, and v2 starts chats on file open and runs tools, which pushes the same way. Consequence: at $0.35 a chat an engaged user costs more than $6 a month on a frontier model, so a sub-$10 all-premium flat plan is underwater for engaged people from the start, and the cheap model or a budget is a launch question, not a later one. With the 2026-10-30 session measurements (Opus 5.5 $0.30 for a simple session, $0.64 for troubleshooting, $1.27 for a complex one, before real pauses), the same floor month costs $5 to $22 at the median of 17.5 sessions and $15 to $65 at the 90th percentile of 51, depending on the mix; on DeepSeek V4 Flash the same months cost $0.26 to $5.40 and $0.77 to $16, with the complex-session figure inflated by slice polling on a debug build. 10. **Grandfathering early payers is cheap.** True at tens of payers by arithmetic.

([[figma-jusprin-v2-file]]). Since 2026-10-20 these artifacts ARE the source of truth ([[design-source-is-claude-artifacts]]); edit them directly. The Figma re-sync steps below are history.

Tools, reads and backups are durable now, outside the repo:
`~/.claude/projects/-Users-kenneth-Projects-JusPrin/figma-mirror/` — start with

scripts that reproduce it byte for byte.

How Kenneth wants a re-sync done (2026-10-13): back up first, re-import, then
compare the backup with the new import so nothing already in sync regresses.
The method that worked, in order:
- rebuild from the old reads and require byte-identical output (proves the
  scripts);
- re-read Figma with the old script and diff the reads (proves Figma unchanged:
  all 14 files were identical);
- only then change scripts, and explain every file `compare_builds.py` reports;
- score every artboard against Figma's own page screenshots
  (`visual_compare.py`) and allow no artboard to score worse.

of Figma (0–255 scale) went from 99 to 122 of 186; all 37 cards and 163 of 166
spec files came out byte-identical; tokens matched Figma's variables exactly.

had added behind dark variants (Figma has none), frames forced dark by a "dark"
in their name (use Figma's `explicitVariableModes` instead), a frame half light
and half dark through a nested mode, sets whose background is a two-stop linear
gradient, Figma's GRID layout (children need their own positions), and small
frames centred in the 40px-minimum artboard instead of top-left.

over them in HTML (give the later siblings `position:relative`); Figma tints
icons with a mask plus a coloured rectangle; the Artifact tool's bulk read
prints small text files into context, so have a background agent do large
backups; a session scratchpad is wiped on restart — never keep the only copy of
tools there; when two reads of a page exist, keep the later one by timestamp.

What the survey of other products (`pricing-case-studies-2026-10.md`) says goes wrong, in one list: people cannot picture what an abstract credit buys; two kinds of credit with different expiry rules confuse everyone; the anger is at the boundary, when something they were doing stops; a balance that drops for reasons they did not cause breeds distrust; "unlimited" with an unstated ceiling is read as a lie once reached.

## Five rules that apply at every point (board 0)

1. **One word, one unit, credits only.** "Credits" (decided 2026-11-01), never coins, never tokens. A balance is a number of credits and nothing else: "562 credits left." Kenneth, 2026-11-02: showing a count of messages beside the credits is confusing; consolidate everything into credits. (Canvas versions up to 71 and my earlier drafts put "That is 612 Standard or 112 Expert messages" under every balance; that was my addition, never his decision, and it is gone.) The translation into messages appears only where the person chooses or is stopped: the picker options, the stop card for the chat's own tier, the pricing page's one sentence, and one scale line under the first-month offer ("An Expert message is 5 credits"). The low-balance notice "About 25 credits left" stays, because there the person needs to know how many turns this chat has left. A price never stands alone: "1 credit" confused Kenneth on sight (2026-11-02), so it is always "1 credit a message", "5 credits a message". Dollars appear only on the page where money changes hands. Plans are Hobby ($10 a month), Workshop ($20 a month) and Pay as you go (the never-expiring pack); never Pro, Plus or Premium.
2. **Credits only move when the person sends a message.** Turns the app starts (the file-opened report, the slice-finished note) are free, and the balance never changes without a message from the person. That one fact is what makes the balance trustworthy; it is stated on the pricing page in one sentence: "Only messages you send cost credits."
3. **Expiring credits are named by what they are, with a date. Bought credits are just "credits" and never expire.** "First-month credits · 62 of 500 left · Expires 1 Dec." "Free Standard credits · 50 of 50 left · Resets 1 Dec · Standard only." "Bought credits · 500 left · Never expire." Never a bare number that mixes them. The draw rule is stated once, in the breakdown: "Expiring credits are used first."
4. **Say the number before the boundary, not at it.** Every ceiling (balance, fair use, expiry) is shown on the way there with a count, so reaching it is never news.
5. **Nothing typed is lost and nothing stops silently.** A message that cannot be sent stays in the composer. (The earlier draft added "with a way to send it anyway"; the design session dropped the phrase on board 0 because a chat now keeps its model, so there is no way to send. That follows from Kenneth's decision but he has not reviewed the wording. The ways forward are to get more credits or, when free Standard messages remain, to start a Standard chat with the typed text carried over.)

- **The cheap tier is "Standard".** Kenneth, 2026-11-02, in the brainstorm session: not "Basic" (the first boards' word, which sells the tier on being the lesser one) and not "Quick" (my suggestion). Every surface uses it: "Standard · 1 credit a message", "Unlimited Standard messages", "Free Standard credits", "50 free Standard credits this month", "New Standard chat", and rule 1's explanation. Canvas version 71 says Standard on every board.

- **A chat keeps its model.** Kenneth, 2026-11-02, board 3b: for now a person cannot switch the model mid-chat. The model and thinking pickers stay in the composer once a chat has a message, greyed, and hovering either shows a two-line tooltip: "A chat keeps the model and thinking level it started with. Start a new chat to change them." and "Each message you send in this chat costs 5 credits." (board 2c). So there is no "Send with Standard" and no "Switch this chat to Standard" anywhere.
- **The app's own turns run on Expert, cost nothing, and do not fix the chat's model.** Kenneth, 2026-11-02, brainstorm session. The turn the app starts when a file opens has to read the plate picture, so it runs on Expert whatever the person would pick; it is free under rule 2; and it does not count as the chat's first message. The person's first message fixes the chat's model, and the greyed pickers follow that message, not the app's note. Without this, every chat that begins with a file would be pinned to Expert before the person could choose, since today the app's note takes the account default and fixes the chat to it.
- **A picture in a Standard chat is dropped, and the attachment row says so.** Kenneth, 2026-11-02, brainstorm session: the Standard model cannot see pictures, and he rejected a long clause in the picker option. The notice lives on the staged attachment itself (point 2).
- **One action outside the pricing page: "Get more credits".** Kenneth, board 3c: at the moment someone runs out they cannot judge a pack against a plan from a button label, so there is no "Buy" beside "Subscribe" in the app. "Get more credits" opens the pricing page, which explains the difference. The one exception is the savings alert (point 7), whose "Subscribe" names one plan and shows the sums.

## The points, in the order a person meets them

### 1. First launch: own key or JusPrin account (boards 1a to 1d)

Where: the Agent setup in Preferences › Agent (the one setup flow, decided 2026-10-23) and the welcome screen.

Kenneth's reaction to the first draft, which put the offer as a small line under "Set up JusPrin": "the most non-obvious way to urge user to sign up". Opinion, as drawn: the offer is the headline on its own surface, "Your first month: 500 credits", with the translation under it, "An Expert message is 5 credits. Your own API key stays free.", and the button names the reward, "Sign in for 500 credits". "Explore first" moves below it. Never "trial" (decided): a trial promises a wall at the end. content.text:
Your message cut off at "serving the". I read it as "serving the goals in the pricing doc": traction measured as active users and time in the app, becoming the default AI harness for slicing, low friction, and collecting feedback worth training on. I critiqued the 34 boards on the canvas page "On boarding experience" (onboarding 00 to 20, the three v1 welcome-back boards, and credits 1a to 1d, 6a, 6b) against those four goals.

**The core problem: the flow asks for commitment before it shows value.** A new person walks through welcome, sign-in, a code or browser round trip, an agent check, an Orca import, a physical-setup confirmation and a project choice before the agent does anything. That is seven to nine screens. The one "wow" the product has, the agent proposing a plan on the person's own model, sits at board 13. v1's data says 41% of people ever had exactly one chat. A wizard this long spends the first session on setup, which is the opposite of the "time in the app" metric.

**Where it falls short, by goal**

- **Sign-in is the first door, which contradicts the doc's own rule.** Board 00 says "Start with account setup. Connect an Agent afterward", and its footer says "Account setup comes first if you want to connect one." The doc says sign-in is not required with your own API key, and board 1b even says "Your own API key stays free", but no board offers a key path. A BYOK person must sign in or go agentless. Boards 01 to 08 also duplicate a sign-in flow that the 2026-10-23 decision moved into Preferences › Agent. The handoff doc already says those links go away. These boards are stale against that decision.
- **The sign-in ask is at the wrong moment.** The highest-intent moment is board 12, where the person types what matters for their print. Asking there ("Sign in for 500 credits to send this", message kept per rule 5) converts a person who already wants something. Asking on board 00 converts a person who has seen a static "EXAMPLE INTERACTION · NOT LIVE" box. Obico's data in the pricing doc points the same way: people convert when they want the next thing, not at the front door.
- **"Explore first" leads to a dead end for the harness goal.** The local path ends at board 19, where the agent pane is a "Set up Agent" placeholder. A person who explores never meets the agent on their own project, so the product never makes its case to the audience most likely to become engaged users, the ones who already slice in Orca.
- **The guided tour runs on a phone stand, not their part.** Boards 11 to 16 walk a "representative mockup" and end with "Open my project", which asks the person to start again. v1 usage comes in project sessions. The tour should run on the file they brought, with the example only when they have none. Board 08, the first-run Home ("Drop a model or project to start"), already has the right one-step shape. The wizard competes with it.
- **Setup steps carry friction with no payoff at that moment.** Board 10 asks the person to go check the plate on their printer during onboarding. The plate matters at slice time. Board 10a hides the one agent-powered setup step, identifying the printer from a photo or the network, behind a fork after "Configure manually". Boards 09, 17 and 18 give the preset import more screens than the first chat gets.
- **The welcome speaks to one audience.** "Your Orca workflow" and "bring along your tuned presets" address the Orca user. The doc says the two audiences converge and the product should be the default harness for both. The person who cannot slice reads a screen about a tool they do not use. The job is a good print, not a workflow migration.
- **Nothing in the flow serves the feedback goal.** No step tells the person their chats are kept, no step learns whether they edit settings themselves (the check the doc names for hypothesis 8), and nothing sets up the one label the doc calls missing, "did the print work". The flow could at least say a report will be asked for after a print.
- **Vocabulary drifts across screens.** Account, Agent, AI access, "JusPrin AI service" and "Agent connected" are five names for one thing within ten boards. "Agent" is never explained to a first-time person, and every local screen's header carries "Local mode · Agent not configured", which frames the local path as deficient.
- **The v1 subscriber boards leave a boundary surprise.** Board 1d moves the 20 most engaged people from unlimited to 750 credits a month and does not say so. The touchpoints doc flags this as open. Under the doc's own rule, say the number before the boundary, this is the place.

**What already serves the goals.** Every error state (03, 05, 07, 19a) keeps the person working with "Continue locally" and never strands them. The first-month offer on 1a to 1d is the headline and the button names the reward. Board 6a ends the first month with no wall and no modal. The v1 welcome-back path replaces boards 01 to 09 for returning people rather than making them repeat setup.

**Recommendation in one line.** Collapse the wizard to the first-run Home: open their file, let the agent's free file-opened turn show something real, and make the sign-in or key ask at the first message, with the import and physical setup deferred to the moments that need them.

content.text:
The constraint is real: the agent cannot say anything until a model answers, and a model needs either a key or an account. But "account first" is only one way to meet it. The question is who pays for the first few turns and when the ask happens. Five options, cheapest to build first.

**1. Move the ask from the front door to the composer, nothing else changes.** First-run Home opens the person's file as today. The chat panel shows the agent is there, with the first-month offer inline: "Sign in for 500 credits and I'll plan this print." The sign-in is one click to Google and back, no wizard around it, and the person lands in the same chat with their file already open. The person sees their own model on the plate and the agent waiting, instead of a welcome screen with a fake example. Value shown: the product, not the agent. Cost: zero model spend. Build: small, mostly removing boards 00 to 08.

**2. Let the app's own first turn run before sign-in.** The gateway already treats app-started turns (the file-opened report) as free. Issue an anonymous device token on first launch and let that one turn run on it. The person opens a file and, within seconds, the agent describes what it sees on the plate and what it would check, then the composer asks for sign-in to continue, with the typed message kept. Value shown: a real Expert read of their actual part. Cost per install: roughly the price of one Expert turn with a plate picture. From the doc's measurements that is on the order of $0.10 to $0.30, calculated, not measured. Build: gateway token issuance, one free turn per token, rate limit per device and IP.

**3. Anonymous starter credits.** Same device token, but it carries a small lot, say enough for two or three person-sent Expert messages. Signing in converts to the 500. The person gets a plan, applies it, maybe slices, and is stopped only at the third or fourth message. By then they have something to lose, which is where Obico's conversion happens in the pricing doc. Cost per install: calculated from the doc's figures, about $0.30 to $0.80 on Opus or $0.15 to $0.35 on Sonnet. Risk: reinstall farming and use of the endpoint as a free model proxy. Both are weak attacks here, because the gateway fixes the system prompt and tools to slicing, and a device plus IP cap holds the spend to under a dollar per abuser. Build: option 2 plus a ledger entry type for anonymous lots.

**4. Own API key as an equal door at the same gate.** The doc says sign-in is not required with a key, but no board offers one. At the composer gate, "Paste an API key" beside "Sign in for 500 credits" makes the Orca power user's path one field, and that person is the loudest early adopter. Cost: zero. Build: the Preferences › Agent key row already exists, so this is a link to it from the gate.

**5. A cheap model for anonymous turns, Expert after sign-in.** Cuts option 3's cost by 10 to 20 times, from the doc's DeepSeek measurements. I would not do it: the first impression is the one impression, and hypothesis 4 (the cheap model is good enough) is untested on the real task. A weak first answer costs more users than it saves dollars.

**My pick: 1 + 2 + 4 now, 3 once 2 is measured.** Option 1 removes the wizard and costs nothing. Option 2 makes the agent's first words about the person's own part before any ask, at a cost of one turn per install, which is the kind of subsidy the doc says you are willing to pay. Option 4 honours the rule you already set. Option 3 is the same mechanism with a bigger number, so turn it on after you see how many people who got the free turn then sign in. None of these blocks profitability later: the anonymous allowance is a number you can set to zero.

One thing to decide alongside: whether the free app turn runs with the plate picture. With it, the first message is specific to their part and worth the spend. Without it, the agent can only talk about settings, which reads like any chatbot.

content.text:
Yes, that is the shape, with one correction and one gap worth naming.

**The correction: it is not "try it for a few messages" by default.** With the version I would ship first, the person gets exactly one free turn before the ask, and it is the turn the app starts, not one they type. The few-messages version is the follow-up once you have seen how many people who got that one turn then sign in.

**How I imagine the first run, step by step**

1. **Launch lands on Home, first-run state.** Empty projects, the line "Drop a model or project to start", an empty printers column. The first-month offer sits on Home as a card, headline and "Sign in for 500 credits" button, visible but not blocking. If an OrcaSlicer configuration is on the machine, one quiet row offers to import the presets in a click. No wizard.
2. **The person drops their own model.** Prepare opens with the part on the plate and the chat panel open. Someone with no file handy gets the bundled example from the same empty state.
3. **The agent speaks first, on their part, before any ask.** This is the free app-started turn, running on an anonymous device token. It describes what it sees on the plate and what it would do, and asks what the part is for. This is the moment the product makes its case, and it costs one turn per install.
4. **The person types their first message. Send is the gate.** The composer says "Sign in for 500 credits to send this" with "Paste an API key" beside it. Their text stays in the box. Sign-in is one click to the browser and back, into the same chat.
5. **From there it is the ordinary flow.** The agent proposes, the person applies, slices, checks the print, then prints or exports. Printer connection, calibration and the rest come up when the work needs them.

**The gap: the printer.** Today the workspace tools need a printer selected before the agent can do anything, and the wizard's boards 09 and 10 existed to get one chosen first. Two ways to close it, and I lean to the second:

- Home asks for the printer before the file opens, one picker, the add-printer form you already have.
- The agent's first turn handles it. If no printer is selected, its first words are "Which printer will this print on?" and the printer-setup tool does the rest, by model name, photo or the network. The wizard step becomes a conversation, which is the product's whole point. This needs a check in the code that the file-opened turn can run with no printer selected. I have not verified that.

**What the person with a file feels.** They launched, dropped their part, and within a minute an agent talked about that part specifically and asked a sensible question. Then they were asked to sign in to answer it. That is the order the pricing doc argues for: value, then the ask at the boundary, with nothing typed lost.

entries.description:
Start a separate Claude Code session for a task while you stay with the user (when: see "Starting other sessions"). `initiation` says who wants it: "user_asked" starts it now and returns its id; "offer" is for a task the user named in their latest message (new work here, or "suggest / split off / make a task or session for X"): called with a title alone, it shows a "New session" / "Do it here" card and WAITS for their answer, so it must be the only call in that message (no update_plan, no other tool); the result then tells you to carry on here, or to send the brief with proposal_id so the session starts; "own_initiative" is for work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — something you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up (when your reply calls work a follow-up or a separate PR, propose it here rather than only saying so, unless it acts on what this session just found and so stays here), never what "Starting other sessions" keeps here or gives to a subagent; the user sees a card and nothing runs until they start it, by clicking it or by telling you (then call this again with just proposal_id).
"user_asked" and "own_initiative" both need a `prompt` — the brief: the task, the files or area, what done looks like — and the call is refused without it; `background` does not stand in for it. Only an "offer" is a title alone.
context: "fork" = this whole conversation + your `prompt`. "fresh" (default) = your `prompt` + `background` only, so `background` is required too, at least 80 characters.
Checkout here ("fresh" only): use_worktree false = shares this checkout and can edit it (in a worktree session its branch and PR too: never for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository); true = its own worktree (the default when this session is in one).
Elsewhere ("fresh", user_asked only, when the user named the place): `cwd`, `target` "ssh" + `host`, `environment` or `preset`; list_start_targets lists the valid names.

initiation.description: "user_asked": the user asked in words for separate, parallel or background work, or told you to start this piece — it starts now (not for a piece "Starting other sessions" gives to a subagent). "offer": a task the user named in their latest message (new work for this session, or one they asked you to suggest, split off or make a session for) — the user is asked first and the call waits for their answer; send only title with it (the brief follows, with proposal_id, if they choose New session). "own_initiative": work you propose yourself that the user has not told you to do — something you noticed, or the follow-up your own answer or work turned up; it waits as a proposal card until the user starts it; never for a task the user's message tells you to do, nor for the one piece of work "Starting other sessions" keeps here, nor for what it gives to a subagent. Required unless proposal_id is set.

proposal_id.description: Start a proposal the user told you to start, exactly as proposed: its task_id and nothing else (wake_when_done may accompany a local one). To change it, dismiss_task it and start a new session.

title.description: Under 60 chars; names the task. Shown on the row or card. Required unless proposal_id is set.

prompt.description: The brief: the task, the files or area, what done looks like. Required for "user_asked" and "own_initiative" — the call is refused without it, and `background` does not stand in for it; an "offer" leaves it out (the card shows the user's own message) and you send it with proposal_id once they choose New session. Here and in `background`, put file paths and code identifiers in backticks.

context.description: "fresh" (default) or "fork" — see the tool description. A "fork" from a worktree session gets a fresh worktree, normally cut from your branch tip (commit first; uncommitted edits stay here); from a plain checkout it shares the folder.

background.description: Required with "fresh", besides `prompt`: at least 80 characters of overall goal, decisions and constraints so far, how this piece fits — for someone who has not seen this conversation. Ignored for "fork".

wake_when_done.description: Once this session (and any sibling still working) ends its turn, or fails to start (unless it waits at a prompt the user answers there, its folder was never opened in Claude Desktop, or the user started, stopped or archived it), and you are idle, the app continues you, whether or not this is set. true also continues you if this session never gets its task some other way, such as a brief that is not sent; default false; not with own_initiative; ignored with target "cloud", which never continues you.

name.description: Optional short handle for the session ([a-z0-9-], ≤24), e.g. "cli-cleanup". Linked sessions and plan steps refer to it by this name; derived from the title when omitted.

use_worktree.description: "fresh" only (rejected with "fork"). false = shares this session's checkout and can edit it (in a worktree session: its worktree, branch and PR, so never for work that ends in a branch or PR of its own or belongs in another repository); not accepted from a session set up to move from the user's checkout into a worktree with EnterWorktree (before or after it moves), a fork of a session working in a worktree on an SSH host, or one whose worktree was given back. At another place named by `cwd`, `host` or `preset`, false = that folder as it is. true = its own git worktree. Omitted: the same folder when this session works in a plain folder and has never had a worktree (its own, a shared one, or one it will enter later); otherwise its own worktree. Omitted with `preset` or `host`, or with `cwd` from a session on an SSH host: the default set on that preset or SSH connection instead.

model.description: "fresh" only, optional: a cheaper model id for mechanical or read-only pieces (e.g. a Sonnet or Haiku id). Same family or cheaper than yours; anything higher is ignored. Omit to inherit yours.

target.description: "fresh" only. "local" (default) = where this session runs. "cloud" = run it as a cloud session (keeps going when this computer sleeps). Needs the repository on GitHub and a cloud environment — the app checks and tells the user if it cannot, and the task then stays as a card for them to start. model/effort/use_worktree/cwd/source_branch do not apply. Only when the user asks for the cloud. "ssh" = on the SSH connection named by host (or by a preset).

host.description: With target "ssh": the name of one of the user's saved SSH connections (as list_start_targets reports it) — never a raw hostname, user or key. The app connects as the user configured it and may ask them to sign in.

cwd.description: The folder the session works in, when it is not this project: an absolute (or ~/) path on the host it will run on — this computer, this session's host, or the SSH connection named by host (default there: the connection's folder). "fresh" only.

environment.description: With target "cloud": the name or id of one of the user's cloud environments (list_start_targets lists them); omitted = the default one.

repository.description: With target "cloud", only when the user named a repository other than this project's: "owner/name" on github.com, which the cloud session clones at its default branch. Take the exact owner/name from the user's words or a listing that shows it; if you are not sure of it, ask them. A bypass or auto permission mode may not carry over: the session then starts in the cloud's default mode. If the call is refused, do not run or propose the other repository's work in this project.

source_branch.description: The existing local branch the new worktree is cut from. Default in this project: this session's base branch (the one picked when it started, or the one its worktree was cut from). If the session has none and either it runs on an SSH host or its project folder is itself a git worktree or submodule, the folder's current commit. Otherwise, the repository's default branch, or the folder's current commit if that is unknown. Only for a session that gets its own worktree (use_worktree true, or the place's default); not with target "cloud".

branch_name.description: A short slug for the new worktree's branch (the app adds the user's branch prefix and a suffix). Only with a worktree.

preset.description: The name of one of the user's saved session presets on this computer: it names the place itself (a folder here or an SSH connection and folder — do not pass host or cwd with it) and brings model, effort and worktree defaults plus its saved environment variables; use_worktree/model/effort override those. Cloud and Remote Control presets are not available here.

effort.description: "fresh" only, optional: reasoning effort at or below yours. Omit to inherit.

permission_mode.description: Optional, local starts only: the permission mode it starts in — this session's own or a lower one (omit to inherit it). A higher mode, or one the app does not offer here, is refused; raising a session is set_session_permission_mode's card to show.

message.content:
> The gap: the printer. Today the workspace tools need a printer selected before the agent can do anything, and the wizard’s boards 09 and 10 existed to get one chosen first. Two ways to close it, and I lean to the second:
> 
> Home asks for the printer before the file opens, one picker, the add-printer form you already have.
> The agent’s first turn handles it. If no printer is selected, its first words are “Which printer will this print on?” and the printer-setup tool does the rest, by model name, photo or the network. The wizard step becomes a conversation, which is the product’s whole point. This needs a check in the code that the file-opened turn can run with no printer selected. I have not verified that.

The most straightforward way is probably to import from orca slicer. Another option is just to add a default printer. If the goal is just to let the user experience asap.

This made me wonder if a completely wizard-free onboarding is optimal. We when we drop straight the user straight into the slicer, what the user can see is a very simple simple user interface, which is a plus, but the value proposition can be revealed until the user discover those themselves. 

My current hypothesis is that some user will be attracted by the fact that they can bring their own keys. Some user will be attracted by just to trying using agent on the slicer and some hardcore users may want to connect this as an MCP server.

content.text:
Three reactions, then a pick.

**The printer gap: agree, and the file itself comes first.** Most 3MFs saved from Orca or Bambu Studio carry their printer preset, and the app already has the "printer from the file" chip for that. So the order is: printer from the file, else import from Orca when it is on the machine, else a default. A default is fine for the first turn as long as the chip marks it as assumed and the agent's first words say so ("I've assumed a Bambu A1 mini; tell me if it's something else"). A silent default is the one version to avoid, because the agent's first sentences about plate size and material would be confidently wrong, and that is the first impression.

**On wizard-free: you are right that a bare slicer hides the proposition, but the wizard was never what revealed it.** The current boards reveal the setup steps. The value is revealed by the agent's first turn on the person's own part. What the bare-Home version loses is the sentence that says what this program is and the moment the person chooses how they want to use it. That is one screen, not nine.

**Your three segments are also three doors, and each door is one step.** That is the strongest argument for keeping a single welcome screen:

- **"Use your own API key"**: a key field right on the card, no account. Done in one paste.
- **"Try the agent, 500 credits in your first month"**: sign in with Google, one browser round trip. This is your 1b offer, as one of three choices rather than the only one.
- **"Connect it to Claude Code or Claude Desktop as an MCP server"**: shows the config snippet and the command, costs you no model spend at all, and is the literal form of "default AI harness for slicing". The server exists already, so this door is mostly documentation.
- A small "Just slice for now" under them, which lands on Home with the agent pane offering the same three doors later.

Every door lands on the same place: first-run Home, drop a file, the agent speaks about their part. The import-from-Orca row and the printer handling stay where I described them, after the file, not before.

**Two things this buys that the wizard-free version does not.** The door a person picks is the segmentation data the pricing doc says is missing: you learn the BYOK, hosted and MCP shares from day one without a survey. And it removes the need for the anonymous free turn to make a first impression, because the BYOK and MCP people never needed one and the hosted person is one click from it. The anonymous turn becomes a later experiment on the hosted door only, if its conversion disappoints.

**My pick.** One welcome screen with the three doors and the pitch in one line, then Home, file, first turn. Not zero screens, not nine.

The design session I started is working from the fully wizard-free brief. If you want this version instead, say so and I will send it the change. If you want to see both side by side, I can ask it for the three-door welcome as an added variant.

## figma
The official Figma MCP server. Use this server whenever the user wants to create, generate, edit, implement, or sync any design, UI, screen, component, mockup, or visual — in Figma, FigJam, Figma Make, or Figma Slides — and whenever the user mentions Figma or provides a figma.com URL.

This server bridges code and design in both directions, and supports designing from scratch using existing design systems and codebases.

FILE SESSION:
Once the target fileKey is known, call create_session with that key and a concise task description before search_design_system, get_libraries, use_figma, or any other file tool. This applies to read-only tasks too. If a new file is needed, call create_new_file first, then create_session with the returned file key. Reuse the returned UUID as the sessionId argument on eligible file tools for subsequent work on that task, including calls to other files.

CAPABILITIES:
- Read designs FROM Figma into code (get_design_context, get_screenshot, get_metadata, get_figjam)
- Write designs INTO Figma from code, intent, or existing components (use_figma, generate_figma_design, create_new_file, upload_assets)
- Bridge code and design via Code Connect (get_code_connect_map, add_code_connect_map)
- Create diagrams and FigJam content (generate_diagram, get_figjam)

WHEN TO USE THESE TOOLS:
- The user wants to create, mock up, or generate any UI, screen, component, or design — even if Figma isn't named
- The user wants to implement a design as code (design-to-code)
- The user wants to push a page, view, or component into Figma (code-to-design)
- The user wants to update, sync, or edit an existing Figma file
- The user shares a figma.com URL
- The user wants to build or extend a design system, design tokens, or component library
- The user wants to create a diagram in FigJam

SKILLS (Prefer the skills shipped with the Figma plugin on the agent being used. If no Figma plugin is installed, use the skills served by the Figma MCP resource):
- /figma-use — MANDATORY before calling use_figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-design — for translating an app page or layout into Figma; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-design/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-library — for building a design system in Figma from code; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-library/SKILL.md
- /figma-code-connect — for mapping Figma components to codebase components; fallback: skill://figma/figma-code-connect/SKILL.md
- /figma-use-figjam — for FigJam-specific use_figma flows; fallback: skill://figma/figma-use-figjam/SKILL.md
- /figma-generate-diagram — MANDATORY before calling generate_diagram; fallback: skill://figma/figma-generate-diagram/SKILL.md
- /figma-design-to-code — MANDATORY before calling get_design_context; fallback: skill://figma/figma-design-to-code/SKILL.md

URL PARSING:
Extract fileKey and nodeId from Figma URLs:
- figma.com/design/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=:nodeId → convert "-" to ":" in nodeId
- figma.com/design/:fileKey/branch/:branchKey/:fileName → use branchKey as fileKey
- figma.com/make/:makeFileKey/:makeFileName → use makeFileKey
- figma.com/board/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=:nodeId → FigJam file, use get_figjam
- figma.com/slides/:fileKey/:fileName?node-id=:nodeId → Figma Slides file

DESIGN-TO-CODE WORKFLOW (Figma → code):
MANDATORY: load the /figma-design-to-code skill BEFORE calling get_design_context — it carries the full workflow (adapting the reference, reusing existing project components and tokens, and honoring the response's hints by priority). After create_session, call get_design_context with the nodeId and fileKey — it is your primary tool; its output is a REFERENCE to adapt to the target project, not final code.

CODE-TO-DESIGN WORKFLOW (code → Figma):
1. Load the /figma-generate-design skill if available.
2. Once the target fileKey is known, call create_session before any file tool; call create_new_file first if a new file is needed. Then ALWAYS call search_design_system as the first design-system lookup to find existing components, variables, and styles to reuse — never ge… [truncated]

entries.name: SendMessage
entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.

input.message:
Kenneth wants two versions of the first-run flow side by side, so add a variant B beside the wizard-free flow you are drawing (variant A), as a second numbered board set on the same canvas page with its own canvas note.

Variant B differs from A in exactly one place: before first-run Home there is ONE welcome screen, and nothing else of the wizard returns. The screen states in one line what the program is (OrcaSlicer's workflow with an agent that plans the print) and offers three doors, each one step, plus a small fourth link:
1. "Use your own API key": the key field is on the card itself, no account; pasting the key is the whole step. (Kenneth's rule: it is "Your own API key", and this path never needs sign-in.)
2. "Try the agent": the first-month offer as already decided, headline "Your first month: 500 credits", under it "An Expert message is 5 credits. Your own API key stays free.", button "Sign in for 500 credits". One browser round trip.
3. "Connect it as an MCP server to Claude Code or Claude Desktop": shows the config snippet or command the app's MCP server already needs (look at how the app exposes its MCP server under `src/slic3r/GUI/JusPrin/` and the `--manual-mcp` flag; draw the real snippet shape, not placeholder text) and costs no hosted spend.
4. A small "Just slice for now" link under the three doors.

Every door lands on the same first-run Home as variant A, and from there the flow is identical (drop a file, printer from the file else Orca import else a default marked as assumed, the agent's first turn on their part). Draw for B: the welcome screen, the state of each door once taken (key pasted and verified; browser round trip and return; MCP snippet copied), and the Home the person lands on, where the agent pane is already live for doors 1 and 2 and shows the three doors again for someone who chose "Just slice for now". Reuse A's boards for everything after Home instead of redrawing.

Also, for both variants, the printer handling order Kenneth settled on: the printer preset inside the 3MF first (the "printer from the file" chip already exists on the canvas's file-printer boards), else import from OrcaSlicer when a configuration is on the machine, else a default printer that the chip marks as assumed and the agent's first words name ("I've assumed a Bambu A1 mini; tell me if it's something else"). Never a silent default.

In the untracked note, add a short comparison: for each variant, the number of screens and clicks from launch to the agent's first words about the person's own part, for each of the three kinds of person (own key, hosted, MCP), and what each variant can and cannot measure about which kind of person arrived. Captures for B go in the same `design-captures/first-run-2026-11/` folder with a `b-` prefix. Send both sets of PNGs with SendUserFile when ready.

The search didn't turn up a primary NN/g onboarding-carousel study. Most of the results are secondhand summaries, and the strongest NN/g evidence is about homepage carousels, not onboarding.

**Nielsen Norman Group findings (via secondary sources)**
- On carousels generally, NN/g reportedly found that people mostly engage with the first slide and largely ignore the rest. Users overwhelmingly interact with the first slide while subsequent slides are largely ignored, according to one summary.
- On app tutorials, one NN/g study reportedly found that people who read the tutorial rated what it taught them as more complex than people who skipped it. Participants who read the tutorials actually perceived what it was teaching them as more complex than people who didn't read the tutorials.
- A 2023 NN/g piece, as described by a blog, says traditional tutorials interrupt users mid-task, aren't memorable, and don't improve task performance. It also attributes skipping to users wanting to get on with the task. It says traditional tutorials interrupt users who are attempting to do something else at that moment, they do not tend to be memorable, and they also do not result in better task performance.

**Other evidence**
- A Notre Dame study, cited by a design blog, found very low carousel engagement. Only 1% of visitors clicked on a slide at all and of those, 84% of clicks were on the first one.
- UX writers describe a "learned blindness" pattern, where users skip carousels on reflex because they've seen so many. Users don't evaluate each onboarding carousel on its own merits. Yes, I understand it, and I underweighted it. The three doors are how the person gets to the agent, not why they came. The thing they came for is "tell it what you want to print and it sets up the slicer", and the boards so far say "your Orca workflow, with help", which is the opposite framing: a slicer first, with a helper attached.

**Should the first launch say it? Yes, but as one sentence and one proof, not slides.**

What I could verify quickly: the research on intro carousels is weak and mostly about web, and the secondhand reports of Nielsen Norman's work say people engage with the first slide and ignore the rest, and that people who read a tutorial rated the product as more complex than those who skipped it ([summary](https://www.dolfy.ai/blog/onboarding-skip-button-problem-first-run-tutorials-ignored), [carousel critique](https://a11ywithdiana.substack.com/p/your-carousel-isnt-showing-more-content)). I could not find a primary desktop study, so what follows about desktop apps is my recollection, not a checked fact: Cursor, Raycast and Linear each open with one screen that states the proposition in a line and asks for the one setup choice they need, then drop you into the product with a live first task. None of them uses a swipe-through. Mobile carousels exist because a phone app cannot show the product until you have granted it things; a desktop slicer can show the product at once.

**So the proposition belongs in three places, all already in the flow:**

- **The welcome headline.** Not "Your Orca workflow, with help planning the print" but the promise itself, something like "Say what you want to print. JusPrin sets up the slicer." The three doors sit under it as the how.
- **One proof under the headline.** A ten-second recorded clip of a real session, a person typing a goal and the plate changing, in place of the static "EXAMPLE INTERACTION · NOT LIVE" box. Real output, not typed mock strings. This does what the slides would do, in one frame.
- **The first turn on their own part.** This is the proof that counts, and the rest only frames it.

I'm sending this to the design session now so both variants carry it: the proposition as the headline on the welcome screen in B and on Home's empty state in A, the clip in place of the fake example, and the Orca-first framing dropped from the copy.

content.content:
## 1. What v1 actually logged

This section comes first because it decides which questions are answerable.

**Per-chat records (`app_jusprinchat`, Postgres).** One row per conversation, linked to the user (`user_id` foreign key, not null). The desktop chat page (served by the Obico server, `obico-server/frontend/src/views/jusprin/v1.2/EmbeddedChatPage.vue`) creates the row on the first AI call of a conversation and then overwrites `messages` with the full JSON message list after every AI reply (`populateDatabaseWithChat`, a PUT). Fields: `messages`, `machine_name`, `filament_name`, `print_process_name` (preset names at the last save), `slicing_settings_json` (unused), `user_feedback`, `user_feedback_text`, `created_at`, `updated_at`. There are 31,566 rows from 2024-10-07 to 2026-10-29, totalling 85 MB.

- **Turns are distinguishable.** `messages` is a JSON array of `{role, content}` objects; all 31,566 rows parse. There are 84,156 user messages and 381,767 assistant messages. Assistant messages carry extra keys that reveal what happened. `slicing_profiles` marks a settings proposal (44,506 of them). `suggested_printing_method` is a "Do your magic" plate analysis, a model call that looks at a render of the plate (20,934). `jusprinNotification` is a slicer warning or error shown in the chat (30,096). `agent_actions` are UI actions the AI asked for.
- **Messages have no timestamps.** Only the chat's `created_at` (first AI call) and `updated_at` (last save) exist, so timing inside a chat is not recoverable from Postgres.
- **History is partial by design.** The "Start over" button starts a new row. Local actions (slicing, export, undo) are never saved unless a later AI call triggers a save. A rejected plate analysis is popped from the list and disappears. Counts below are therefore lower bounds on activity.
- **Button text and typed text share one field.** Quick buttons push localized canned sentences as user messages. I separated "typed" messages with a heuristic: a message counts as typed unless its exact text came from 3 or more different people, or its first 30 characters came from 20 or more people. By that rule, 58,603 of the 84,156 user messages are typed.

**AI-call counter (`app_jusprinaicredit`).** There is one row per Obico account (251,031 rows, because a signal creates one for every new Obico user since 2025-07-04). `ai_credit_used_current_month` resets on the 1st of each month (celery task `reset_monthly_ai_credits` in `web_ent/app_ent/tasks/jusprin_tasks.py`) and is never incremented for unlimited (paying) users, so it holds no history. Today 251,009 rows have quota 50 and 22 have -1 (unlimited). The October 2026 snapshot was used once, to validate the AI-call estimate (section 2).

**Plan state (`jusprin_jusprinplan`).** There are 33 rows, one per user, holding only the latest state: plan id, Chargebee ids, and `expired_at`, which is set at cancellation and cleared on reactivation. History lives in Chargebee.

**Chargebee.** This was reachable. The pod's configured Chargebee client answered read-only `Subscription.list`, `Invoice.list` and `Plan.retrieve` calls. It holds 42 JusPrin subscriptions, each under its own customer record, with status, activation, cancellation and cancel reason, plus their invoices.

**Per-request records.**
- **Postgres** has none. There is no request log, token count, model name or subscription flag per request. `middleware.py` only switches the response language, and `responses_transport.py` only translates requests between two OpenAI API formats; it records nothing.
- **Langfuse Cloud** (`us.cloud.langfuse.com`, set up in `obico-server/backend/app/jusprin/views.py`) does trace every AI call, with `userId`, `sessionId` (= chat id, on some traces), timestamp, latency and model input/output. It only reaches back to 2026-07-31: 12,622 traces, so the retention is about 90 days. I confirmed it is reachable with two read-only GETs but did not pull it, because the Postgres data already answers the timing questions.

**Behavioural events.** v1 sent none to the server. The desktop app's slice, export, print and apply-settings actions run locally through `callAgentAction` and are never reported back. I checked every server call in the v1.0 and v1.2 chat pages: `me`, `chats`, `chats/messages`, `plate_analysis` and `contact_support`. The only behavioural traces are indirect:
- slicer warnings saved in the message history;
- whether a plate analysis was accepted as-is or edited;
- prints recorded by Obico for the 773 chat users who also connect a printer to Obico.

**Other JusPrin tables.** Postgres has exactly three JusPrin tables (`app_jusprinchat`, `app_jusprinaicredit`, `jusprin_jusprinplan`). An older `JusPrintChat` table in `app_ent` (migrations 0036–0039) was dropped in 0044.

**User-to-chat link and timezone.** Every chat has a user. Local time is known only for the 1,212 chat users whose Obico mobile app reported a timezone (`app_mobiledevice.preferred_timezone`); everything else is in UTC.

How the inventory was taken: `inv.py`, `fmt.py`, `fmt2.py`, `pr.py`, `cb.py` (appendix), plus reading the files named above in `/Users/kenneth/Projects/tsd-enterprise`.

## 2. Usage
## 5. Feedback and behavioural signal

### 5.1 Explicit feedback is rare

Source: `main.py`, section "Feedback".

- Of 31,566 chats, 14 have a thumbs rating (8 positive, 6 negative) and 2 have written text. The ratings come from 12 people; paying users left none.
- By year: 9 ratings in 2024, 4 in 2025 and 1 in 2026.
- The two comments in full: "It helped me with what I need and want to do. It helps." (positive, 2024-12) and "Não é explicativo." ("It isn't explanatory", negative, 2026-02). Neither is specific.
- The rating UI was never in the slicer. It sits on the Obico web app's G-code file page (`frontend/src/components/g-codes/JusprinFeedback.vue`), so a person only saw it after uploading G-code to Obico.
- The ratings may also be attached to the wrong chat. That page asks for the chat by `g_code_file_id`, but the chats API ignores that filter and returns the user's newest chat, so any rating lands on whichever chat was newest at the time.

### 5.2 Behaviour inside the chat history

Sources: `main.py`, sections "Plate analysis outcomes" and "Behavioural proxies".

Fields: `messages`, `machine_name`, `filament_name`, `print_process_name` (preset names at the last save), `slicing_settings_json` (unused), `user_feedback`, `user_feedback_text`, `created_at`, `updated_at`. There are 31,566 rows from 2024-10-07 to 2026-10-29, totalling 85 MB.

- **Turns are distinguishable.** `messages` is a JSON array of `{role, content}` objects; all 31,566 rows parse. There are 84,156 user messages and 381,767 assistant messages. Assistant messages carry extra keys that reveal what happened. `slicing_profiles` marks a settings proposal (44,506 of them). `suggested_printing_method` is a "Do your magic" plate analysis, a model call that looks at a render of the plate (20,934). `jusprinNotification` is a slicer warning or error shown in the chat (30,096). `agent_actions` are UI actions the AI asked for.
- **Messages have no timestamps.** Only the chat's `created_at` (first AI call) and `updated_at` (last save) exist, so timing inside a chat is not recoverable from Postgres.
- **History is partial by design.** The "Start over" button starts a new row. Local actions (slicing, export, undo) are never saved unless a later AI call triggers a save. A rejected plate analysis is popped from the list and disappears. Counts below are therefore lower bounds on activity.
- **Button text and typed text share one field.** Quick buttons push localized canned sentences as user messages. I separated "typed" messages with a heuristic: a message counts as typed unless its exact text came from 3 or more different people, or its first 30 characters came from 20 or more people. Good, this is the right order: the proposition decides the headline, the proof clip, and even the door order. Here is how the two candidates compare, using what v1 recorded.

**Candidate A: a much simpler way to slice.** "Say what you want to print and the app sets up the slicer."

- **Who hears it:** the person who finds slicers hard. Mostly the second audience, people who cannot slice in Orca today.
- **The download moment:** a new printer, a new model, no idea which settings matter.
- **What it competes with:** the default profile. For a Bambu owner the stock profile already prints fine, so "simpler" is an answer to a problem they rarely feel. It bites hardest on non-Bambu printers, multi-material and odd models.
- **What v1 says:** people used the plate analysis heavily, 14,591 chats, and accepted it verbatim 12,666 times. But v1 was built as a setup tool, so this measures what the product offered, not what attracted them.
- **Risk:** the Orca crowd, your first audience, hears "dumbed down". A simplification claim is also easy for Bambu or Orca themselves to copy with better defaults.

**Candidate B: expert help with a printing problem, now.** "An expert who can see your project, tells you what went wrong, and fixes the settings, instead of waiting for a forum reply that may never come."

- **Who hears it:** everyone who has had a failed print, which is both audiences. A beginner and an Orca veteran both have stringing at eleven at night.
- **The download moment:** a specific, timed, emotional one. A print failed, they posted a photo, and nothing came back. That moment motivates a switch in a way "simpler" does not. That is my reasoning, not a measured fact.
- **What it competes with:** the subreddit, Discord, and asking ChatGPT. The sentence that beats ChatGPT is "it can see your file, your settings and your slice, and it applies the fix". That is the one thing a chat window cannot do.
- **What v1 says:** the correction signal is there even in a setup-oriented product. About one typed follow-up in six reports what happened on the printer or tells the agent it was wrong, around 3,000 messages, and the redo pattern has about 1,000 same-object chats returning between six hours and a week later, which is the shape of "printed it, came back to fix it". The messages themselves are the proposition in the person's words: "I printed this file and it still strings a lot", "still the same corner blobbing".
- **Risk:** it promises help the slicer cannot always give. Half of failed prints are hardware: clogs, belts, bed. An expert saying "that is a clog, not a setting" is still real help, but the promise has to include that honesty, and the proof clip should show a diagnosis, not only a settings change.

**How they relate.** B is the better reason to download. A is the better reason to stay. A person who comes in with a failed print and gets it fixed inside the slicer then slices the next model here too, and that is where "default harness" and time in the app come from. Led the other way round, a person who came for "simpler" has no reason to open the app when the print fails, because nothing told them it could help with that. B also fits the tier names you already chose: Expert is "troubleshooting, tricky models, anything you'd ask a person".

**What this changes in the flow.** The headline becomes the problem, not the workflow. The proof clip shows a photo of a bad print going into the chat, the agent naming the cause and changing a setting, the re-slice. The first turn on the person's own part still works, with one addition: when the file is a 3MF that has been sliced before, the agent can open with "Has this one printed well, or is there something to fix?" And B tells you where the first users are: the fix-my-print threads are the channel, which no amount of "simpler" copy would have told you.

**Cheap ways to test rather than argue:** classify the first typed message of every v2 chat as setup or problem once the gateway is live. Watch which door people take. And if you ever run a landing page, the two headlines are the A/B.

The design session is currently drawing the A headline, "Say what you want to print. JusPrin sets up the slicer." I will hold it there until you pick, then send the change.
